transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi, doctor. Gosh, it's actually really hard to say out loud now that I'm sitting here. I’ve been going back and forth for weeks on whether I should even make this appointment because, you know, I work down at the department store—I’ve been in retail sales for years—and I'm on my feet all day, dealing with customers, so I'm always exhausted anyway. I just kept telling myself I was fine, just stressed out. 

But... well, what finally scared me into actually coming in to see you today is about what happens after I eat. Sometimes I just eat way too much, far more than I ever intended to, and I get so absolutely terrified of putting on weight. You know how it is, at 66, the metabolism just isn't what it used to be, and you have to be so careful. So... I've been going into the bathroom afterwards and making myself throw up. I do it so I won't gain the weight from everything I just ate. 

I kept telling myself I wouldn't do it again, that it was just a moment of weakness. I really thought it was just going to be a one-time mistake, you know? Just a foolish thing I did because I was panicked. But it’s gotten to where it isn’t just a one-time mistake anymore. It's become this whole awful routine, and honestly, it just terrifies me that I'm doing this to myself at my age. I just didn't know who else to talk to about it.
How often do you have these episodes where you eat way too much?

Oh, well, that's... gosh, that's the part that really made me realize I needed to be here, sitting in this chair, talking to you. Because, like I said, I really thought I could just stop. I told myself, "Barbara, you're 66 years old, you know better than this, just don't do it again." But then I'd be at home, usually after a long shift at the store where my feet are just aching and customers have been running me ragged, and I'd start eating. And before I knew it, I'd eaten so much, and the panic would set in again. 

If I really sit down and look at it, and be completely honest with myself—which is hard, doctor, it really is—it's been going on for at least the past several months. And it's not just every once in a great while, either. It's most weeks. Most weeks I have at least one of those... those secret eating spells, where I just lose all control, and then I have to go into the bathroom and make myself sick afterward. I keep trying to brush it off, but when it's happening most weeks for months on end... well, I just can't honestly call it occasional anymore, can I? It's become a habit, a terrible, terrifying habit, and I just don't know how I let it get this far.
Do you do anything else to try to counteract the weight gain after these episodes of eating too much, besides making yourself throw up?

Well, no, not really. I mean, making myself sick is awful enough, isn't it? I don't take any of those diet pills or laxatives or anything like that, if that's what you mean. I've heard stories about young girls doing all sorts of crazy things, but I don't do any of that. And as for exercise... well, like I said, I'm on my feet all day at the department store. By the time I get home, my ankles are swollen, my back aches, and I'm just completely drained. The absolute last thing I have the energy for is putting on sneakers and going for a jog or whatever people do. 

I just... I just rely on throwing up. Gosh, it sounds so terrible when I say it like that, just plainly out loud. It makes me feel so ashamed. I keep thinking about how my mother would react if she knew. She was always so proper, you know? She'd be horrified. But no, to answer your question, doctor, it's just the throwing up. I don't try to fast for days or run miles or take pills. I just panic, and I go to the bathroom, and I undo what I just did. And then I wash my face, rinse my mouth out, and try to pretend it never happened. Until the next time, anyway.
Do you ever eat way too much without later making yourself throw up?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I suppose there might have been a time or two, way back when this all first started, where I just felt so miserably full and guilty but managed to talk myself out of going to the bathroom. But lately? No. Honestly, doctor, the panic just takes over completely. 

It’s like... once I realize how much I've eaten, my heart just starts pounding, and I can almost feel the weight attaching itself to my hips and my stomach right then and there. It's a dreadful feeling, just dreadful. I sit there on my sofa—it's this lovely floral sofa I bought a few years ago, very comfortable for my bad back—and I just stare at the empty wrappers or the plates, and the guilt is so heavy I can hardly breathe. I tell myself, "Barbara, just sit here. Just digest it, it's fine." But I can't. I just can't. The anxiety builds up until I feel like I'm going to jump out of my own skin if I don't do something about it immediately. 

So, no, if I have one of those awful spells where I eat all those things I shouldn't, I always end up in the bathroom. It’s like a compulsion, like I have to erase the mistake before it becomes permanent. I just can't sit with that feeling of fullness anymore, it terrifies me too much.
Do you worry about gaining weight when you're not having one of these episodes of eating too much and then throwing up?

Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, I do. It's... it's practically all I think about sometimes, doctor. It's not just when I'm having one of those terrible spells, not at all. It's a constant, nagging little voice in the back of my head. 

I mean, just the other day, Sunday morning, I was getting ready for church. I've been going to the same Methodist church for forty years, and I always try to look nice, you know, presentable. So I was putting on this navy blue skirt—it's a very sensible skirt, a-line, usually quite flattering—and as I was zipping it up, it just felt... snug. It felt tight right across my stomach. And doctor, my heart just sank right into my shoes. I stood there in my bedroom, holding my breath, looking in the mirror, and I just wanted to cry. I almost didn't go to service at all. I spent the whole time sitting in the pew, tugging at the waistband, convinced that Reverend Miller and the choir and everyone else was looking at me and thinking, "My goodness, look how Barbara has let herself go." 

And it happens at work, too. I'll be walking past one of those big, full-length mirrors we have in the ladies' apparel section—they put them everywhere so the customers can see themselves, but they're just dreadful for me—and I'll catch a glimpse of my side profile. Just a quick glance, and it completely ruins my entire day. I see my stomach, or my hips, and I just feel this overwhelming sense of disgust. I'll spend the rest of my shift trying to suck my stomach in, hiding behind the cash wrap, just feeling so heavy and awful. It's exhausting, it really is. I just feel like my weight and my shape are the only things people see when they look at me, and I'm so terrified of getting any bigger. So, yes, the worry is there all the time, even when I'm not eating. It never really leaves me alone.
Do you think you would still be afraid of gaining weight if you were at a weight that most people would consider normal?

Well, I... I really don't know, doctor. I'm honestly not sure what to say to that, because I don't even know what a "normal" weight means for me anymore. I mean, what is normal, really? 

I remember going to Dr. Henderson—he was my general practitioner for years and years before he retired, a very sweet man, always wore these colorful little bowties—and he had one of those height and weight charts taped to the back of his exam room door. According to that chart, I suppose I've been all over the place in my life. But even when I was younger, say in my thirties or early forties, and I was wearing a size eight... which all the ladies I work with at the department store would tell you is a perfectly lovely, normal size for a woman my height... I still worried constantly. 

I'd like to think that if I just reached some magic number on the scale, or if I woke up looking like one of the mannequins I dress in the misses department, all this fear would just vanish. But I just don't know if it would. I look back at photographs from my niece Sarah's wedding—oh, it must be fifteen years ago now, they had a beautiful outdoor ceremony by a lake—and I had on this lovely peach pantsuit. I remember feeling so dreadfully heavy that day. I was so self-conscious I wouldn't even eat a single bite of the wedding cake, and it was lemon raspberry, my absolute favorite. But when I look at those pictures now? I was perfectly normal! Trim, even! I looked nice. 

So if I was terrified of gaining weight back then, when I looked just fine to everyone else... I really don't know if being at a "normal" weight now would actually make the fear go away. It’s like the worry is just baked right into my bones at this point. I wish I could give you a simple yes or no, I really do, but I just can't be sure. It just feels like no matter what size I am, that little voice in my head telling me I'm too big is always going to be there.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past few months?

Well, I... no, not really. I mean, not anything significant, anyway. It's actually incredibly frustrating, doctor, because I step on the scale—oh, I must step on that thing three or four times a day sometimes. I keep it right next to the bathtub on the tile floor. I actually just bought a new one last month, one of those fancy digital ones with the clear glass top? The old one I had, the one with the little red dial, well, if you leaned just a fraction of an inch to the left or the right, the needle would move a pound or two, and it was just driving me absolutely out of my mind with the uncertainty. So I got this new one, and... well, to answer your question, the number just sort of hovers right around the exact same place it always does. 

Maybe it goes up a pound or two after a bad weekend, or down a pound on a Tuesday, but... no major changes. Which is almost worse, in a way! Because I put myself through all this... this absolute turmoil, all the eating and then the panicking and rushing to the bathroom, and worrying constantly about my stomach and my hips, and for what? I'm not gaining, thank heavens, but I'm certainly not losing anything either. 

Just the other day I was unpacking a shipment of the new spring slacks at the store—they're doing a lot of pastels this year, very pretty soft yellows and mint greens, though they show every single lump and bump if you aren't careful—and I was looking at the size tags while I was putting them on the hangers, just thinking, "Barbara, you're going to be in the exact same size you were last spring, and the spring before that." It's like my body is just stuck. So, no, no real changes over the last few months. Just the exact same number staring back at me every single morning, no matter what I do.
Do you worry about gaining weight on days when you don't have one of these episodes of eating too much?

Oh, well, like I was telling you just a little bit ago, doctor... yes. Oh, heavens, yes. It really doesn't matter if I've had one of my spells or not, the worry is just always sitting right there on my shoulder. 

I think I mentioned my navy blue skirt earlier? The one I wear to church? It's exactly like that. If I'm getting dressed for Sunday service and that skirt feels even the slightest bit tight around the middle, it just completely ruins my whole day. I'll go to church, but I can't even focus on Reverend Miller's sermon because I'm just sitting there in the pew, pulling at my waistband, and I just feel like everyone around me can tell I’ve let myself go. I start thinking the ladies in my Bible study are whispering about it. 

And it's the exact same thing at work. If I'm walking through the misses department and I just happen to catch my side view in one of those big store mirrors... well, that's it. The day is ruined. Even if I haven't eaten a single thing that I shouldn't have, just seeing that reflection makes me feel so heavy and exposed. I'll spend the rest of my shift just agonizing over it, feeling like every customer I ring up is judging me. So, yes, even on a perfectly good day, that fear of getting bigger is just constantly, constantly on my mind.
Do you think you look overweight when you look in the mirror, even when others might say you look fine?

Well, doctor, I... I think I've touched on this a bit already, but yes. Absolutely, yes. It's just like I was saying about that navy blue skirt for church, or catching my reflection at the store. It really doesn't matter what anyone else thinks or says, because when I look in the mirror, all I see is... well, I see someone who is just too big. 

Just last week, my friend Susan—we’ve known each other since our girls were in brownies together, oh, that must be thirty-some years ago now—she came into the store to look for a mother-of-the-bride dress. Her youngest is getting married in October, a lovely fall wedding up in the mountains. Anyway, Susan looked at me and told me I looked wonderful, that I hadn't aged a day, and she even asked if I'd lost a few pounds. And she's a dear friend, she wouldn't just say it to flatter me, but... I couldn't believe a word of it. I just smiled and thanked her, but inside, my stomach was in knots. 

Because I know what I see. If that skirt feels even a tiny bit snug around my waist before Sunday service, or if I catch that side view in the big three-way mirrors we have by the fitting rooms... oh, it just ruins my whole day. I feel so heavy, so... so wide. I just feel like everyone around me can tell I’ve let myself go, no matter what Susan or anyone else says. I'll spend the entire day pulling at my clothes, trying to hide my stomach, just feeling absolutely dreadful about myself. So, yes, even if people tell me I look fine, the person I see in the mirror is... well, she's definitely overweight, and it's just so hard to shake that feeling.
Do you think your weight or body shape is the main thing that determines your self-worth?

Well, doctor, I... I know I keep coming back to this, but it really is just like I said before. It's... it's everything. I mean, if I'm getting ready for church and that navy skirt feels even a fraction of an inch too tight around my middle, or if I happen to catch my side view in one of those big mirrors at the store... well, it just completely, utterly ruins my whole day. And I don't just mean I feel a little bad about it, I mean it consumes me. 

Because when I feel like that, when I feel heavy or wide, I just... I feel like I have no value at all. I feel like everyone around me can tell I've let myself go, like they're looking at me and judging me, and... and if I can't even keep my own body in check, then what good am I? I know it probably sounds silly to someone like you, but my whole mood, my whole sense of whether I'm a good person or a failure, it just all hinges on how my clothes fit and what that scale says. If I feel thin, I feel like I can take on the world. But if I feel big... well, I just want to hide away from everyone. So, yes, I suppose it really is the main thing. It's the only thing, sometimes.
Do you think your weight or body shape is abnormal, even when others tell you that you look normal?

Well, doctor, I... I know I must sound like an absolute broken record today, going on and on about the exact same things. I really do apologize for that, but... well, yes. Yes, I do think it's abnormal. People can say whatever they want to try and make me feel better—just like my friend Susan did the other day—but it honestly doesn't change what I feel in my own skin. 

It all just comes right back to what I've been saying. If that navy skirt feels even the slightest bit tight before church, or... or if I happen to catch my side view in that awful store mirror... it really doesn't matter who tells me I look normal, because it will still just completely ruin my whole day. I just feel like everyone can tell I’ve let myself go. To me, it doesn't look normal at all; it feels like this... this glaringly obvious, abnormal flaw that everyone must be staring at. 

I’ll be at work, you know, just standing there ringing up a nice lady buying a blouse, and she might say something sweet to me, but inside I’m just thinking, 'Oh, you're just being polite, I know you can see how wide and out of shape I am.' I just can't accept that I look normal when everything I see and feel tells me that I'm just entirely wrong. It just takes over my whole mind, and I can't shake the feeling that they're all just pitying me.
Do you think your perception of your body shape and weight is accurate?

Well, doctor, I... I know I'm probably exhausting you by saying the exact same things over and over again, but... I mean, I really do think what I'm seeing is the truth. I know you're asking if my perception is accurate, and... well, yes, I believe it is. It has to be, doesn't it? Because it's what I live with every single day. 

It just always, always comes back to that same feeling. Like I said, if I'm getting ready for church on Sunday morning—and Sunday mornings are usually so lovely, my husband makes coffee and the house is quiet—but if I put on that navy skirt and it feels even the tiniest bit tight around my middle, or... or if I'm at work and I catch my side view in that big three-way mirror by the fitting rooms... well, it just completely ruins my whole day. And I don't mean it just makes me a little sad, I mean it just destroys me. Because when I see that, when I feel that tightness, I just know that everyone else can see it too. I feel like everyone can tell I've let myself go. 

I just... I can't imagine that what I'm seeing and feeling is wrong, because it feels so incredibly real to me. I'll be standing there at the register, trying to smile and ring up a customer, and all I can think about is how wide I look, how heavy I am, and how obvious it must be to every single person who walks through those doors. So, yes, I do think my perception is accurate, because if it wasn't, why would it affect me so deeply? Why would a tight skirt or a passing glance in a mirror have the power to just completely ruin my entire day and make me feel so exposed? It just has to be the truth, doctor, I really believe that.
Do you think your fear of gaining weight is related to how you see your body, rather than your actual weight?

Well, doctor, I... I know I keep saying the exact same thing, and I'm so sorry, I really am, I must sound like a broken record by now. But it really is all connected, isn't it? It's like I can't separate the fear from what I see in the mirror or how my clothes feel. 

It just... it all goes back to that navy skirt, you know? Like, if I'm getting ready for church, and Sunday mornings are usually my favorite time, but if I pull that skirt up and it feels even a fraction of an inch tighter than it did last week... or, heaven forbid, I catch my side view in that big mirror at the store while I'm working... it just completely, utterly ruins my whole day. And it’s not because I stepped on a scale and saw a number. It's because of how I look to myself in that moment, how wide and out of shape I feel. 

When I see that, or when I feel that tightness, I just panic. I get so afraid because I feel like everyone around me can tell I’ve let myself go. I'll be standing there at the register, and I just know everyone is looking at me, judging me, seeing exactly what I see in that awful store mirror. So, yes, I suppose the fear really is tied to how I see myself, how I feel in my own skin, rather than what an actual scale might say. It’s just that the feeling is so overwhelming, it just takes over everything.
Do you think your actions after eating, like making yourself throw up, are more about how you feel about your body rather than the actual food you've eaten?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose you're right about that, yes. It's not really about the food itself, is it? I mean, I know I just go on and on about the same things, and I do apologize for talking your ear off today, but... well, it all ties back into exactly what we've been saying. It's about how I feel in my own skin, how terrified I am of letting myself go even further. 

You see, what finally scared me into coming in to see you—and it took a lot for me to make this appointment, I really went back and forth on it for weeks, talking to my husband, worrying about what you might think—but what finally did it is that... well, after I eat too much, after I just lose control like that... I've been going into the bathroom and making myself throw up. I just do it so I won't gain weight, so I won't get any wider than I already feel when I look in that awful store mirror. 

And the thing is, doctor, it’s gotten to where it isn’t just a one-time mistake anymore. At first, I told myself, 'Oh, it's just this once, you just overdid it at dinner, it won't happen again.' But then it happened again, and again, and... and it's just become this terrible cycle. Because if I don't do it, I just sit there thinking about how my clothes are going to fit, how that navy skirt is going to feel on Sunday morning, and the panic just completely takes over. I just can't stand the thought of the food sitting there, turning into weight, making me look even more out of shape to everyone around me. So, yes, it’s absolutely about how I feel about my body. The food is just... it's just the thing that triggers all that fear and disgust I have when I look at myself.
Do you think you would still make yourself throw up after eating if you didn't care about your weight or body shape?

Well, doctor, I... I don't think I would. I really don't. If I didn't care about how I looked, if I didn't care about my weight or my shape... well, why would I put myself through all of that? It's awful, it really is. It makes my throat hurt, and my eyes water, and I always worry my husband will hear me in the bathroom, even if he's all the way downstairs watching his programs. 

But I do care. I care so much it just consumes me. Like I keep saying—and I know I keep saying it, I know I'm probably wearing you out with the same story—but it all comes back to that feeling. If I didn't care, then putting on that navy skirt on a Sunday morning wouldn't matter, would it? If it was tight, I'd just think, 'Oh well, I'll wear something else,' like a normal person. But I'm not like that. If it feels tight, or if I'm at work and I happen to catch my side view in that big three-way mirror by the fitting rooms... well, it doesn't just bother me a little. It ruins my whole day. My entire day is just gone. 

Because the second I see that, or the second I feel that waistband digging in, I just feel like everyone around me can tell I’ve let myself go. I feel like every customer I ring up, every person I pass in the aisle, they're all just looking at me and thinking about how heavy I am. If I didn't care about any of that, if I didn't have this constant, overwhelming fear of what people are seeing when they look at me... no, I definitely wouldn't make myself sick. I wouldn't need to. It's just... it's the only way I know how to fix it, to stop myself from getting any bigger and feeling any worse when I look in that mirror.
Do you think you would still feel the need to control your weight if you couldn't see yourself in mirrors or reflections?

Well, doctor, that’s... that’s an interesting way to think about it. If there were no mirrors anywhere at all... I suppose I wouldn't have to see that awful reflection at the store, which would be a blessing, honestly. But... no, I don't think it would stop me from needing to control it. Because, well, I know I’m just repeating myself again, and you must be so terribly tired of hearing about my wardrobe by now, but it really wouldn't fix the problem. 

Because it's not just about seeing the reflection, is it? It's the feeling. Like I was saying before about getting ready for church. Even if all the mirrors in my house were covered up on a Sunday morning, I can still *feel* my clothes. If I pull that navy skirt up and the waistband is digging into my waist, even just a fraction of an inch... it just completely ruins my whole day. I don't even need a mirror to know it's tight. And the panic sets in exactly the same way. 

Because even if *I* can't see my reflection, everyone else can still see me, can't they? Whether it's catching my side view in that store mirror or just feeling the tightness of my skirt in the church pew, the result is exactly the same. I just sit there, or I stand at my register, feeling absolutely certain that everyone around me can tell I’ve let myself go. They don't need a mirror to see that I'm heavy, they just look right at me. I feel like they can see every bulge, every place where the fabric is pulling. So, yes, I'd still be just as terrified and feel just as much of a need to do something about it, because I'd still feel the clothes on my body, and I'd still just know that everyone else is looking at me and judging me.
Do you think you would still try to control your weight if everyone around you thought you were at a perfectly healthy weight?

Well, doctor, if everyone around me thought I was perfectly healthy... oh, I don't know. I mean, my husband, bless his heart, he tells me all the time that I look fine, that I shouldn't worry so much. He'll say, 'You look wonderful, dear,' when we're getting ready for church, but... but it doesn't really matter what he says, does it? Because I know how I feel. 

I know I just keep coming back to this, and I'm sorry to keep harping on the same things, but it’s just the truth of it. Even if every single person at the store, every customer, every person in the congregation on Sunday morning told me I looked perfectly healthy... if I go to put on that navy skirt and it feels tight, or if I happen to catch my side view in that terrible three-way mirror at work... it just completely ruins my whole day. It doesn't matter what anyone else says, because *I* feel it. I feel the waistband digging in, and I see the reflection, and I just feel like... well, I feel like everyone can tell I've let myself go, regardless of what they might be saying to my face to be polite. People are polite, you know? They don't want to hurt your feelings. But I can feel it. I can feel the tightness, and the panic just washes over me all the same. So, yes, I think I would still try to control it, because I just can't stand that feeling of... of being out of control and letting myself go like that.
Do you think you would still try to purge after eating if you didn't have a distorted view of your body shape?

Well, doctor, if I didn't have a distorted view... if I just saw myself the way I actually am, or the way other people say I am... well, I suppose that goes right back to the root of it all, doesn't it? If I could just look in the mirror and see a normal, healthy sixty-six-year-old woman, maybe things would be different. But I don't. 

I know I've said this to you three times already, and I really am sorry for talking your ear off about my clothes and my job, but it's just the only way I know how to explain it to you. It's like... if I didn't see myself this way, then maybe catching my side view in that terrible three-way mirror by the fitting rooms wouldn't be such a catastrophe. But right now, with the way my mind works, the second I see that reflection, or the second I try to put on that navy skirt for church and it feels even the slightest bit tight around my middle... it just completely ruins my whole day. My entire day is gone before it even starts. 

Because when I feel that tightness, or when I see that angle in the mirror, I don't just think, 'Oh, I've gained a pound.' I feel this overwhelming certainty that everyone around me can tell I've let myself go. I feel like the customers at the register are staring at me, like the people in the pews are whispering about me. So if I didn't have that... that distortion, as you call it... if I could just put on a tight skirt and think nothing of it, then no, I don't think I'd need to make myself sick. I wouldn't have that horrible panic driving me to the bathroom to try and undo what I just ate. But because I do see myself this way, because that feeling of being heavy and judged is so real to me... well, I just can't seem to stop.
Do you think you would still have the desire to eat excessively if you didn't have the fear of gaining weight afterwards?

Well, doctor, that’s... that’s a very good question, and honestly, it’s something I’ve laid awake at night thinking about. If I wasn't so terrified of the weight, would I still eat like that? I suppose... I suppose I might still have the urge, but it wouldn't feel quite so frantic, if that makes sense. Because the way it happens now, it's just so out of control. 

Take my bridge nights, for instance. Or even when I get off a late shift at the store. You know how exhausting it is, standing on your feet for hours, dealing with customers who are upset because their coupons expired, scanning item after item... By the time I get home, the house is so quiet, and my husband is usually asleep, and I just feel this sort of emptiness. And I'll go into the kitchen, just intending to have a little snack, maybe a cracker or two. But then... then I just start eating, and I can't seem to stop. 

I'll pull out the leftover casserole from the fridge, and I won't even heat it up, I'll just eat it cold standing right there at the counter. And then I'll remember the cookies I baked for the church bake sale—I always make extra, just in case—and I'll eat three or four of those. Then I'll move on to a whole sleeve of crackers, maybe with some cheese, and then a bowl of ice cream on top of all that. I eat all of it in one single sitting, doctor. It's so much food. It's much, much more than I would ever, ever put on a plate if anyone else was in the room. If my husband walked in, I'd probably die of shame right there on the linoleum. 

So, if I didn't have the fear of gaining weight... maybe I wouldn't eat quite so much in secret like that. Because half the time, I think I eat that way because I know I shouldn't, and the guilt just makes me eat more, and then the panic sets in about the navy skirt fitting, and... well, it's a vicious cycle, really. But the amount of food I eat during those times, it's just shameful. It really is. I don't know what comes over me.

I’ve been going back and forth for weeks on whether I should even make this appointment because, you know, I work down at the department store—I’ve been in retail sales for years—and I'm on my feet all day, dealing with customers, so I'm always exhausted anyway. I just kept telling myself I was fine, just stressed out.

So, yes, I'd still be just as terrified and feel just as much of a need to do something about it, because I'd still feel the clothes on my body, and I'd still just know that everyone else is looking at me and judging me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a distorted body image
doctor.question: Do you think you would still try to control your weight if everyone around you thought you were at a perfectly healthy weight?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: If my skirt feels tight before church or I catch my side view in the store mirror, it can ruin my whole day because I feel like everyone can tell I’ve let myself go.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about whether the patient's need to control her weight is dependent on others' perceptions, which directly relates to her body image disturbance and how weight/shape influences her self-evaluation.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, if everyone around me thought I was perfectly healthy... oh, I don't know. I mean, my husband, bless his heart, he tells me all the time that I look fine, that I shouldn't worry so much. He'll say, 'You look wonderful, dear,' when we're getting ready for church, but... but it doesn't really matter what he says, does it? Because I know how I feel. 

I know I just keep coming back to this, and I'm sorry to keep harping on the same things, but it’s just the truth of it. Even if every single person at the store, every customer, every person in the congregation on Sunday morning told me I looked perfectly healthy... if I go to put on that navy skirt and it feels tight, or if I happen to catch my side view in that terrible three-way mirror at work... it just completely ruins my whole day. It doesn't matter what anyone else says, because *I* feel it. I feel the waistband digging in, and I see the reflection, and I just feel like... well, I feel like everyone can tell I've let myself go, regardless of what they might be saying to my face to be polite. People are polite, you know? They don't want to hurt your feelings. But I can feel it. I can feel the tightness, and the panic just washes over me all the same. So, yes, I think I would still try to control it, because I just can't stand that feeling of... of being out of control and letting myself go like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a distorted body image or an actual fear of weight gain
doctor.question: Do you think you would still try to purge after eating if you didn't have a distorted view of your body shape?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: If my skirt feels tight before church or I catch my side view in the store mirror, it can ruin my whole day because I feel like everyone can tell I’ve let myself go.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question is asking whether the patient's purging behavior is driven by a distorted view of her body shape, which directly relates to the undue influence of body weight or shape on her self-evaluation.

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, if I didn't have a distorted view... if I just saw myself the way I actually am, or the way other people say I am... well, I suppose that goes right back to the root of it all, doesn't it? If I could just look in the mirror and see a normal, healthy sixty-six-year-old woman, maybe things would be different. But I don't. 

I know I've said this to you three times already, and I really am sorry for talking your ear off about my clothes and my job, but it's just the only way I know how to explain it to you. It's like... if I didn't see myself this way, then maybe catching my side view in that terrible three-way mirror by the fitting rooms wouldn't be such a catastrophe. But right now, with the way my mind works, the second I see that reflection, or the second I try to put on that navy skirt for church and it feels even the slightest bit tight around my middle... it just completely ruins my whole day. My entire day is gone before it even starts. 

Because when I feel that tightness, or when I see that angle in the mirror, I don't just think, 'Oh, I've gained a pound.' I feel this overwhelming certainty that everyone around me can tell I've let myself go. I feel like the customers at the register are staring at me, like the people in the pews are whispering about me. So if I didn't have that... that distortion, as you call it... if I could just put on a tight skirt and think nothing of it, then no, I don't think I'd need to make myself sick. I wouldn't have that horrible panic driving me to the bathroom to try and undo what I just ate. But because I do see myself this way, because that feeling of being heavy and judged is so real to me... well, I just can't seem to stop.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's behavior is driven by a fear of gaining weight or a distorted body image
doctor.question: Do you think you would still have the desire to eat excessively if you didn't have the fear of gaining weight afterwards?

target_item.name: Eating_Large_Amount
target_item.manifestation: After a bridge night or a late shift, I might come home and eat leftover casserole, cookies I baked, crackers, and ice cream all in one sitting, much more than I’d ever put on a plate in front of anyone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my desire to eat excessively, which directly corresponds to the symptom of eating a large amount of food (binge eating).

patient.answer:
Well, doctor, that’s... that’s a very good question, and honestly, it’s something I’ve laid awake at night thinking about. If I wasn't so terrified of the weight, would I still eat like that? I suppose... I suppose I might still have the urge, but it wouldn't feel quite so frantic, if that makes sense. Because the way it happens now, it's just so out of control. 

Take my bridge nights, for instance. Or even when I get off a late shift at the store. You know how exhausting it is, standing on your feet for hours, dealing with customers who are upset because their coupons expired, scanning item after item... By the time I get home, the house is so quiet, and my husband is usually asleep, and I just feel this sort of emptiness. And I'll go into the kitchen, just intending to have a little snack, maybe a cracker or two. But then... then I just start eating, and I can't seem to stop. 

I'll pull out the leftover casserole from the fridge, and I won't even heat it up, I'll just eat it cold standing right there at the counter. And then I'll remember the cookies I baked for the church bake sale—I always make extra, just in case—and I'll eat three or four of those. Then I'll move on to a whole sleeve of crackers, maybe with some cheese, and then a bowl of ice cream on top of all that. I eat all of it in one single sitting, doctor. It's so much food. It's much, much more than I would ever, ever put on a plate if anyone else was in the room. If my husband walked in, I'd probably die of shame right there on the linoleum. 

So, if I didn't have the fear of gaining weight... maybe I wouldn't eat quite so much in secret like that. Because half the time, I think I eat that way because I know I shouldn't, and the guilt just makes me eat more, and then the panic sets in about the navy skirt fitting, and... well, it's a vicious cycle, really. But the amount of food I eat during those times, it's just shameful. It really is. I don't know what comes over me.
